title: 10: Courts in Authoritarian Regimes
text: Why do authoritarian rulers build (independent) courts? This week we look at what courts do for authoritarian regimes, such as keeping officials in line, reassuring investors and prosecuting opponents. We also consider how the same courts can apply the law in ordinary cases and defer to the regime in political ones.

title: Seminars
text: Seminars are discussion-based. Each week we discuss the mandatory readings, which are chosen to be in conversation with one another and sometimes in open disagreement. Every student is expected to come having read and thought about the readings and to be ready to take part.

title: Seminars
text:
How the seminars work

Come prepared. Read all of the week’s mandatory readings and make notes on paper, which you bring to the seminar, as the use of electronic devices is not allowed in the classroom. The guidance below explains what to look out for and how to prepare.
Introducing the readings. At the start of each seminar a randomly selected student is asked to summarize the readings briefly and to introduce the key debates between them. This takes a few minutes and requires no slides, only the notes everyone should have prepared anyway. The discussion builds from there, with students asked in turn to set out an argument, respond to it and weigh the evidence behind it. Everyone should come ready to speak.
No laptops or phones. Electronic devices are prohibited in both lectures and seminars. This is a deliberate choice to protect concentration and the quality of discussion. It does not apply if your Summary of Reasonable Adjustments (SORA) requires the use of a computer or a similar device in the classroom. Bring the seminar readings on paper.
Attendance is mandatory and monitored by the Department of Political Science. You need to tap your student card when entering the room to register your attendance.

title: Seminars
text:
Reading for the seminar
The length of the mandatory reading list is kept modest so that students have more time to dive deeper into specific topics of interest, which is essential for the final paper in particular, as it needs to be grounded in existing academic literature. The theories and methodologies used in the mandatory and optional readings should also be approached as a source of inspiration for the final paper.
The reading list contains different types of articles, not all of which offer a good template for the final paper:

Review articles give an overview of a field: what has been argued, what the evidence says so far and where the open questions lie. They are a shortcut into a literature and the place to start when a topic is new to you.
Empirical articles are the core of the module. They ask a specific question, propose a theoretical explanation and test it against evidence. These are the readings where we can really get into the detail of research design and results, and they are the model for the final paper.
Conceptual and theoretical pieces appear in a few weeks. They define a concept, set out a normative argument or build a framework rather than test a hypothesis. Read them for the clarity and usefulness of the argument and ask what evidence would count for or against it.

title: Seminars
text:
What to look out for
For each mandatory reading, each student should be prepared to discuss in the seminar the following questions:

what is the main theoretical problem the paper aspires to contribute to?
what observed phenomena are the authors trying to explain?
what is the theoretical explanation of the observed phenomena the authors advance?
what are the key concepts and how are they measured?
what is the empirical approach and what are the strengths and weaknesses of the research design?
what are the findings and in what ways do they support or contradict previous studies?
how would you improve or extend the paper’s research design?

A good way to prepare is to write half a page on each reading answering these questions, and a few lines on how the readings relate to one another. Write these notes on paper and bring them with you, since you will not be able to use a device in the seminar. That is all the introducing student needs and it is what everyone else should have in front of them to be ready to interact.
Many of the empirical readings use advanced quantitative or qualitative methods. We do not expect every student to understand every technical detail of every paper, and the seminar is not the place to work through estimation techniques. What matters is the logic of the study: the theory and concepts, the empirical approach and research design, the findings and their implications for the literature and for policy. If you can explain what the authors compare with what, why that comparison is informative and what they found, you understand enough to take part fully.

In addition to the mandatory readings, each week’s page lists optional readings which constitute a good starting point to the literature on the topic. These are not exhaustive: there are other papers and books on every topic, and further readings are featured in the lecture slides. They are a natural place to start when looking for a topic for the final paper.

title: POLS0113: Judicial Politics
text:
Description
This course provides a detailed exploration of judicial politics across a variety of political systems. As predominantly non-majoritarian institutions, both domestic and international courts have become increasingly contested in recent years. We will seek to understand the importance and behaviour of courts from different angles: judiciaries’ place in democratic theory, the design of judicial institutions, and judges’ interactions with other political actors and society more broadly. Among others, we will be delving into why and how politicians balance delegating decision-making to courts with constraining their room for manoeuvre through appointment procedures and threat of override. We will also compare the institutional features of judiciaries across different political contexts, from democracies to autocracies and from presidential to parliamentary systems. The aim is to equip students with a clear understanding of courts as both subjects and objects of their political environment.

Before spending time on collecting your own data, make sure to check whether an existing database cannot be leveraged for your research question.
More generally, going beyond existing databases when working on the final paper is encouraged but not strictly required. Original data collection can constitute an important contribution, however.

Data tips

in general, more granular data is preferred to aggregated data because it enables attending to potentially important details. For example, having data on judicial decisions at the individual case level is more useful than a monthly summary of how many decisions a given court rendered. The latter can be constructed from the former but not vice versa
when using the texts of judicial opinions (decisions) as data, it is important to keep in mind the limitations of and necessary assumptions for basing inferences on them. The text of a judicial opinion is unlikely to be a sincere representation of the full deliberation and process that led to the decision. In contrast, it is quite likely that the judicial opinion is written as a form of motivated reasoning to justify the court’s preferred outcome. The choice of what is (not) included in the final opinion can therefore be highly strategic. It is very likely that the text (including citations) does not contain the full set of considerations which shaped the judicial outcome
given the limitations of using judicial opinions, empirical research frequently focuses on judicial outcomes. Regardless of the reasoning revealed in the judicial opinion, outcomes of court cases are generally expected to be consequential, at least for the parties to the case and potentially beyond. The most consequential outcomes tend to be dispositions that reveal which party won the case, whether someone was found guilty of a crime, the length of a prison sentence, etc. Less obviously, a case outcome may also be the creation or amendment of a legal rule

title: Assessment
text:
The module is assessed by one compulsory research paper of 3000 words worth 100% of the final mark. The deadline and submission instructions for the assessment can be found on the module’s Moodle page.
The research paper must be empirical in nature. This means the research has to rely on observable evidence to answer a question about an aspect of judicial politics. The research design devised to answer the research question can be quantitative, qualitative or mixed.
The best research questions will follow from and attempt to contribute to scholarly literature on a phenomenon of broader theoretical interest. Even when the paper’s empirical part focuses on just a single case study, it should be made clear what broader phenomenon the case is meant to be an instance of. The research question should result from the identification of a research gap in the literature. The answer to the research question should not be obvious or found in existing academic work.
The introduction to the paper should explicitly motivate why the phenomenon of interest is important (socially, politically, economically, normatively) to study. The introduction should also explain what the key issue or puzzle which need investigating is.
Each research paper must include one section discussing theory and one section discussing research design. The theory section sets out the researcher’s expectations about the studied phenomenon on the basis of existing academic literature and typically ends with a testable hypothesis. The research design section describes how the research question will be answered and must include a discussion of the information (data) and the method (e.g. process tracing or regression analysis) used to produce evidence in support of (or against) a hypothesis. The theory and research design need to be selected so as to be appropriate to the research question.
The findings produced by the empirical analysis should be presented in a separate section for clarity. Thereafter they should be discussed in terms of the hypothesis, the research question and finally related back to the scholarly literature to which the paper is contributing. It is highly recommended to provide additional detail about the empirical analysis in an appendix for the sake of transparency.1
Papers are expected to use an author-year (in-text) citation system. Citation and reference formatting should follow the Chicago style. The list of references at the end of the document are not counted towards the word limit (but the in-text citations are). Any footnotes or endnotes count towards the word limit. Compliance with university plagiarism policies is a must.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Before reaching out over email please make sure your question is not already answered below or elsewhere on this website.
Can my final paper reuse some of the research done for other coursework at UCL?
Only to an extent. The final paper for this module needs to be substantially different from any previously submitted work. If you are planning on reusing previous work, you must flag this to the instructor.
Are the classes going to be recorded?
No.
Can I record the video, image or sound of the classes on my own device?
No.
Are the lecture slides available?
Yes. They are published on the week’s course page shortly before each lecture.
Is class attendance compulsory?
Seminar attendance is mandatory and monitored by the Department of Political Science. You need to tap your student card when entering the room to register attendance.
Can I consult my choice of a topic for the final paper with the instructor?
Yes, during office hours.
Can I ask questions about my paper idea after the term is over?
No. Consultations on paper ideas must take place during the ten teaching weeks.
Is there a +-10% tolerance around the word count for the final paper?
No. The paper can be no longer than 3000 words, excluding the bibliography but including in-text citations.
Do I have to use quantitative methods in the final paper?
No. Qualitative methods are equally admissible, but they should not be confused with a carte blanche to disregard methodological questions. The paper needs to be rigorously empirical in focus.
Can I submit the final paper with an appendix?
Yes. Supplementary analyses – such as robustness checks – or evidence which would take up too much space in the paper – such as a long excerpt from a document – can be submitted in an appendix and referred to in the main text. The appendix does not count towards the 3000-word limit. All essential information must be included in the paper, however.
Is it sufficient to cite literature from the suggested reading list in the final paper?
No. The paper needs to use the most relevant and up-to-date scholarship available on the topic it addresses. This does not mean that literature from the suggested reading list is excluded, but it is unlikely to be sufficient by itself.

title: 1: The Origins of Courts
text: What are courts and what is their purpose in society and politics? In this session we reflect on the intended functions of courts in societies, their history, common typologies of courts and why they are relevant for the study of politics. We also trace where the institutions we recognise today came from, from ancient dispute settlement to the medieval origins of the common and civil law traditions.

title: 3: How Judges Decide I: Theories and Preferences
text: Court rulings have an impact on individuals, economies and political systems. In principle, judgments follow from legal rules. But how do judges make decisions in practice? This week we review the most influential theories of judicial behaviour, the conditions under which they apply and the evidence produced in their support. We also look at how judges’ preferences are measured and how they manifest in decisions across a variety of political and judicial contexts.
